posts.text: The best way to test an email validator is on emails you already know are real. Not a sample file. Not the vendor's demo list. Your own interested replies from last week. Somebody who wrote back "yes, I'm interested" has proven their address is a live inbox with a human reading it. So if a validator grades that address catch-all or invalid, you caught it being wrong, and you can count how often. 1. export everyone who gave you a positive reply in the last week or two. that's your answer key. 2. run those through the validator you use today. anything that comes back catch-all or invalid is a miss you can prove. 3. do the same thing on a fresh pull from a provider like Prospeo, then watch the actual bounce rate in production. that's the other half of the picture and it's the half people skip. 4. cost-benefit it for your own volume. I ran ours against Lead Magic, 500 addresses, about a day and a half of positive responses. 14.6% of them graded catch-all, and we throw catch-all in the garbage, so that whole slice would have been deleted off a normal list. Lead Magic validated them. Most validator comparisons are people arguing about brand. This one is just a number you can check, and the answer key is already sitting in your replies folder. I'll drop the short video with the numbers in the comments.
posts.headline: The best way to test an email validator is on emails you already know are real.

posts.text: Yesterday, I opened my inbox to see one of the best emails I've ever read. It was from our son's basketball coach. He's been coaching the game for 30 years. Yet, every single word of it translates to the world Sales teams are living in right now. A world where AI proficiency is being touted as the holy grail of great salesmanship. A world where sellers have stopped thinking and starting buying into the hype that AI thinks better than they can. A world where appeasing our VC/PE's AI wet dreams is somehow more important than appeasing our customers. Here are my favorite parts of the email. I loved his message. I hope you enjoy it as much as I did. Jen The game our kids are entering is very different from the one many of us grew up watching or playing. The industry has created an environment where families are often encouraged to chase rankings, championships, social media attention, and exposure. I would encourage parents to ask themselves: Is my child actually improving, or just playing more games? Is my child being taught how to think and make decisions? Is my child learning to contribute when not scoring? Is my child developing confidence and learning to handle adversity? Is my child becoming a better teammate and more coachable? These questions matter much more than a ranking or a weekend tournament result. One of the biggest differences between average players and those who continue advancing is their understanding of the game. Can they recognize advantages? Can they defend? Can they make decisions under pressure? Can they play without the ball? Can they accept a role that may be different from what they are accustomed to? The goal should never be to simply create the appearance of success. The goal should be to help young people become genuinely better.

posts.text: This morning, I'm running a Sales team workshop on how to engage VP+ execs. A pic of Oprah, speaking at Harvard's 201 graduation ceremony, is my opening slide and story. Here's why. Oprah did 35,000+ interviews across her 25 years of hosting the Oprah Winfrey Show. Everyone from Beyonce, to Michael Jackson, Obama, George Bush, Whitney Houston, to Tom Cruise. In her speech, she spoke about the most important thing she learned after all of those years of interviewing celebrities and public figures. As soon as the camera went down, almost every guest asked some form of the same question. "Did what I say mean anything?" Presidents. Celebrities. The most famous of the famous. All of them cared about feeling seen, heard and understood. In Sales, we have this tendency to put executives on a pedestal. We think of them as figures, not people. We flex our biggest vocabulary. We speak in dry business language. Yet, they're the same people who drank 4 beers while watching the Brewers win last night (GO BREW CREW). The same people who spent the weekend cheering on the sidelines for their kid's basketball team. The same people who have 32,372 photos of their dog on their camera roll. The same people who have hobbies and nicknames their friends gave them. And, the same people who posted on LinkedIn and get 11 likes. Or, who write an article that they're worried no one saw or read. Or, who had a major career win that they're proud of. Execs are no different than Oprah's guests. They value being seen, heard, and understood. ESPECIALLY when it's clear that you, a human, put thought into them. Not an AI bot. They can almost always tell. I've always been a believer that the best sellers are pretty damn good marketers, too. Because if you want to stand out to a VP+ exec - you have to stand out amidst the 1000 other sellers who want their attention, too. Being memorable matters.

posts.text: I spoke to a Sales leader this week. She joined a new company 2 months ago. She's meeting with their existing vendors to evaluate which contracts she'll renew, which ones she'll expand, and which ones she'll cancel. She had 3 renewal convos this week. Guess how many of those convos left her wanting to renew or expand? 0. She works for a large company. Two are 6-figure contracts, one is 5-figures. They're well-known, "AI-pilled" vendors. You've see them on stages talking about how they've optimized their Sales orgs with AI. And, everyone sits in the audience ooh-ing and ahh-ing and thinking, "We better do this, too". And, yet, we don't stop and ask, "Do these tactics make the experience better for the buyer?". Call me a luddite (I've been called a lot worse), but I think the most important quality in a Sales leader operating in this "Look....a squirrel! Look...a squirrel!" AI era we're living is restraint. OpenClaw! Go buy Mac Minis! AI SDRs! Fire the SDRs! Agentforce! Automate everything! Muse! OMG have you tried it?! Instinct! It's changing the game! ChatGPT/Claude! Use it for everything! A Sales leader can't be the talking dog, Doug, from the movie Up. Yes, it's great to experiment. But, being AI-pilled doesn't equate to making the buyer experience better. And, every time you send a "we should be doing this, too" message to the team, you risk distracting them from what actually matters. How they're showing up in buyer interactions. One of the easiest ways to win right now is to outperform in the Sales conversation. Whether that's new logo, renewal, or expansion. Win on the ability to offer an experience that leaves the buyer thinking, "Wow, they came prepared. That was an insightful and useful conversation". Win on reducing their effort to make the case to renew you or buy you. Win on giving a shit about what their business is trying to achieve (vs. just pointing them PowerPoint slides, dashboards, and usage reports and telling a usage story). I'm all for AI that makes the buyer experience better. There are so many ways it can. But, FFS, you don't need to come home from a conference this week and implement every AI tactic you saw someone present on a stage. Buyer experience > everything.
posts.headline: I spoke to a Sales leader this week.

posts.text: I'm working with a $55m arr tech company Found 2 reasons why their outbound wasn't converting. Here's the fix: 1. Personalization. I get this is controversial and against every 2026 playbook - show me you know me works, but it needs to be done with the simplest and shortest copy possible. For complex b2b, this wasn't possible. We removed all personalization and went straight to the offer. Template: "If we could [Improvement] your [product] - would you be interested? Examples: "If we could cut your churn in half without adding CS headcount in 45 days" "If we could cut your onboarding time in half" "If we could 3x your expansion revenue in 60 days" "If we could build you 3 ai agents for free" 2. Buying triggers were receiving cold email (only). Just because a company is ready to buy, doesn't mean you'll be able to reach them by email. It also doesn't mean their are ready for a conversation. Let's say you're product is a CS chat bot that drives expansion revenue. And your Buying Trigger is found that your target company is Hiring a first VP of Customer Success. You have a 60 day window to convince the VP to replace their current tool with yours. If you think an email drip is all you need to get the meeting - your SOL 98% of the time. Here's the real playbook: 1. Buying trigger is identified 2. Auto-enrich the account with current tech stack - find the chatbot they are currently using ( Sumble is great for this) 3. Run competitor displacement ads for the first 90 days the VP hired 4. Sequence the email drip 5. On day 45, create a pattern interrupt. For this deal (yes it's real), we gifted a coffee cart outside their office - "Your chatbot can't do this either." The CCO and Head of sales were serving up the coffee. 6. Find the champion (never decision maker) and run an incentive program Playbook: signal id > enrich > air cover ads > pattern interrupt > champion incentive This is how you win when you're not the market leader. All the marketers out there - drop a comment on your most creative campaign ⬇️

posts.text: I ran GTM at a $23M SaaS We grew 43% when we measured sales and marketing against the same metric: Pipeline Velocity = (Qualified Opps × Win % × ACV) / Sales Cycle Length Constraint ownership: ↳ Qualified opp volume drops → Marketing owns the 7-day fix ↳ Win rate drops → Sales diagnosis ↳ ACV drops → Check discounting first. Discounts up = Sales. Discounts flat, smaller logos = Marketing is sourcing the wrong segment ↳ Cycle length stretches → Sales analyzes stage by stage (pre-meeting = Marketing) ↳ Everything drops at once → ICP mismatch (joint war room) Here is the exact RevOps architecture we used to scale from $16M to $23M ARR in 16 months: 1 // The CRM Object Model: Fit + Signal Tiers Most CRMs are graveyards of unworked leads with no account context. We restructured the account object into 3 operational tiers and rolled every lead up to it: ↳ Tier 1 (Active Demand): Full ICP fit + 2 verified buying triggers in last 30 days. Routed directly to SDRs who reached out within 1hr ↳ Tier 2 (Fit, Low Signal): enrolled in stage-matched ABM air cover and nurture tracks ↳ Tier 3 (Signal, Poor Fit). auto-DQ to preserve SDR capacity We required two fields on every target account: ↳ Committee Coverage Score: number of buying roles mapped out of the total for that segment. No deal moves past discovery with fewer than 3, and a single-threaded deal in Stage 3+ triggers a manager review. ↳ Trigger Timestamp (hiring surges, new tech install, leadership change) 2 // Routing & Speed-to-Lead Automation ↳ Inbound speed-to-lead: in our data, leads touched in <1 hour converted 2.8x better than leads touched after 24 hours ↳ Outbound rules: SDRs never reach out off cold lists. They sequence only when the account is Tier 1 and trigger is under 72 hours old ↳ Pre-call enrichment: Clay auto-populates the likely economic buyer and technical evaluator onto the account ahead of disco call, so the AE knows who to multi-thread toward. 3 // The Monday 9am Operating Cadence Every Monday morning, leadership received 3 dashboards: Report 1: GTM Efficiency ↳ Magic Number: annualized net new ARR ÷ prior-quarter S&M spend. ↳ CAC Payback by segment: Mid-Market came down from 15 to 11 months. ↳ LTV:CAC by channel: scale at 3:1, breakeven is 2:1, kill anything that stays under 2:1 for two quarters. Report 2: Funnel Health ↳ Pipeline coverage by segment: 3x SMB, 4x Enterprise, reviewed against next-quarter quota↳ Deal aging: automated alert when an opportunity exceeds 2x average stage duration↳ Concentration risk: flag when 1 deal represents >25% of total pipeline Report 3: Forecast Accuracy ↳ MAPE score by segment ↳ Bias detection: identifies consistent sandbagging vs optimistic forecasting ↳ Slippage risk: deals with no champion touch in the last 14 days. posts.text: VP of Sales: "We're losing to competitors" So I read all 35,000 of their closed lost deals. Not one was tagged competitor. When a revenue number misses, the default suspects are always product, lead gen, or the competition. Then you open the CRM activity logs. On their largest deals, over 18 months: ↳ The median won deal took 13 contact attempts ↳ The median lost deal stopped at 5 ↳ The median disqualified deal stopped at 3 But here's the part that actually matters. With the same deals and size band, the only variable was who owned them: ↳ Top rep: 34% win rate ↳ Team average: 19% ↳ Shared inbound queue: 5% ↳ No owner assigned: 0% The deal didn't decide. The routing did. 55 of those deals were worth $694k combined and were never assigned to anyone. Median contact attempts: zero. They won none of them. And the ones that die don't get closed out. A deal they win closes in 36 days. A deal they lose sits open for 165 days before anyone marks it dead. So reps spend months staring at bloated pipeline, convincing themselves coverage is fine, working deals that died last quarter. Here's the fix: 1 // Fix routing before you fix reps ↳ Kill the shared inbound queue for anything above your ACV threshold & assign it to a human on arrival. ↳ Audit unowned pipeline weekly. Zero is the only acceptable number. ↳ Reassign books held by departed reps within 48 hours, not "eventually." 2 // Enforce persistence thresholds Deals we invested in closed at roughly 10x the rate of deals we didn't. Some of that is that good deals attract effort. Some of it isn't. ↳ Validation rules so opportunities can't be marked closed-lost below a minimum touch count. ↳ Multi-channel, not single-channel bursts. ↳ Track average contact attempts per opportunity by rep, and coach on the gap. 3 // Age out the rot When dead pipeline sits open for 165 days, forecast accuracy is fiction. ↳ Alert the moment a deal exceeds 2x average cycle time. ↳ Stage duration limits: advance it or disqualify it. ↳ Route abandoned accounts back to nurture instead of letting them decay in open pipeline. You don't need more top-of-funnel to hit the number. You need the pipeline you already have to reach a human and a minimum # of touch points per deal. Sales and revenue leaders, what's your minimum touch count before a rep can close something out?

posts.text: A moment with my twins reminded me why most GTM outbound fails. When things get chaotic, the natural reaction is to jump toward whoever is screaming the loudest. The loud scream is just noise. Reacting only to volume means missing the quiet signal of what actually needs fixing. Most revenue teams run their pipeline strategy the exact same way. Everyone buys intent data, CAC is up, and SDR response rates drop. Teams rely on packaged intent platforms where dozens of competitors see the exact same surge score on Tuesday morning. When dozens of competitors see the exact same surge score, every team reaches out to the same buyer with the same message. The buyer gets flooded. Domain reputations burn. Reps waste time chasing phantom interest from a dashboard surge that led nowhere. Packaged intent data is the loud noise. Custom buying signals are the quiet operational indicators that actually turn into pipeline. We closed a $173k deal from a hiring signal no tool tracks because we built our own detection system. Here is how custom signal tracking works: A. Tracking specific tech stack requirements in job descriptions ↳ Look past open job titles ↳ Track the underlying architecture and tools listed inside job requirements ↳ When an account specifies required systems, route directly to outbound B. Champion migrations within 72 hours ↳ Track previous champions and buyers from closed-won accounts when they change companies ↳ Connect early in their tenure before new tooling decisions get locked ↳ Reach out before competitors even register account activity C. RevOps headcount ratio ↳ Track when target accounts shift their operational headcount ratios ↳ Headcount ratio adjustments point to pipeline bottlenecks, reporting friction, or GTM restructuring ↳ Outbound lands when leadership is actively working to solve the problem Fit without signal is a cold list. Signal without fit is noise. If you're not reaching out within 72 hours of a trigger, you're too late. What custom buying signals is your team tracking that off-the-shelf tools miss?

posts.text: My twins started preschool this week. I did not expect to get emotional about it. I knew my wife would be. A few days before, it hit me too. Two and a half years old and out the door. The night before, the school ran a parents only session. Slideshow. Schedule. Policies. Nap procedure. Very organized. Very robotic. I walked out thinking these people have their act together. I was not reassured. Not really. Then came the first day. Parents were still in the room, so I got to watch the teachers work. They were not running the slideshow. They were watching. Reading each kid. Clocking what pulled them in and what shut them down. Adjusting before anything went sideways. An hour in, one of them told me something about my son I had never put into words. That was the moment I got calm. The slideshow was the pitch. The first day was the evidence. I have been hired 9 times to fix a revenue number that was missing target. The candidate who presents well and the operator who steadies the ship are not the same person. Most exec teams find that out in month 6. Here is what actually separates an experienced operator from someone who interviews well: 1 // They do not need domain expertise to move the needle Helpful, not required. Pattern recognition travels. Category knowledge can be bought in 60 days. 2 // They evaluate fast, then decide Short diagnostic window, then calls. Not a 90 day listening tour that produces a deck. 3 // Their early calls are better than 80% right You will know by day 45. Write the decisions down. Score them. 4 // When they do not know, they have the confidence to see it through The tell is not certainty. It is what happens when they are wrong in week 6 and still have it fixed by week 10. Anyone can be good in month one. The job is months 3, 6 and 9. And here is what most exec teams are not seeing. You are watching revenue miss. That part is easy to see, it shows up on a slide. What does not show up is the confidence draining out of the team. Quarter after quarter of leadership not knowing how to fix it, until the org quietly stops believing anyone will. Missed targets are recoverable. Distrust compounds. Keep the wrong leader in the seat, or hire the fourth replacement in three years, and entire departments go into a spiral you cannot hire your way out of. Question for the operators here: What was the earliest real signal you got that a leadership hire was wrong?

posts.text: Clay is ruining cold email. Take it from someone who spent 4 years sending 300+ outbound emails every single day. Outbound used to be about finding what resonated. You tested a core pain point, measured the response, and refined the message. Today, I watch outbound teams build massive Clay tables to hyper-personalize They scrape every detail they can find on a prospect, generate custom copy for every lead, and hit send. Then the campaign falls flat, and they have no idea why. Start with the offer. Then personalize. Here is the cold outbound testing hierarchy that books me consistent 3.7% positive replies: 1// Test the offer first Find an offer that pulls before writing custom copy. ↳ Keep copy standardized across the test cohort ↳ Zero deep personalization beyond basic account fields ↳ Test distinct value propositions against each other ↳ Run each offer until you establish a clean baseline Target: ~1% baseline positive reply rate on a standardized email. If an audience will not respond to the core offer with standard copy, personalizing the first sentence will not save it. Example: “Would you be interested if I built you a contact list of your past clients who just changed jobs and aren't working with you yet?” 2// Hyper-personalization testing Personalization does work, but it needs to be standardized and tested thoroughly. If you run offer testing against 100+ daily sends, pair it down to 10 per day. This will give you the ability to hyper-customize. ↳ Do a ton of research on the person, a little nugget about them and mention it to them in email, super casual.↳ Then find them on all social platforms possible (Instagram, LinkedIn, X, Facebook)↳ Message them on all those platforms to give you a higher probability of being seen.↳ This takes 10 outreaches per day and 3-4x’s it. ↳ Copy and paste the same message and say “btw I reached out to you via email also” This is how you hit 25% reply rate on a small list. Same impact as 100+ emails per day. 2// Personalization + Offer = Scale ↳ Keep the winning offer and call to action identical ↳ Your manual personalization work will help you ID the 2-3 types of customized messages that work. Wrap them around a specific pain or buying trigger (Clay is great for this part!) Target: scale reply rates up to 3-5%.With buying triggers I see positive replies above 6%. Testing constraints: 1 // Cohorts ↳ 1 industry ↳ 1 buyer committee role ↳ 300 contacts per test cohort ↳ 2 emails per contact 2 // Send limits ↳ Never hit the same contact with more than 1 offer per month ↳ Tag every record with the offer version and cohort outcome This testing system means: - You know exactly which offer generates pipeline - Personalization scales a working message instead of hiding a weak one This is the rigor that outbound teams need.

posts.text: I run a Meta / Google ads agency exclusively for (high) 8 & 9-figure brands. I'll be the first to say AEO is IMPORTANT. A quick 101 guide in case you haven't made any changes: 1. Map the buying decisions → A buying decision is anything a shopper settles before they buy, across discovery, comparison, objections, fit and care. → Pull 20-30 questions from support tickets, reviews, site search and post-purchase surveys, in the shopper's wording. → Example: "best polarized sunglasses for driving" (discovery), "[brand] vs [competitor]" (comparison), "is [brand] worth the price" (objection), "will [frames] fit a wide face" (fit), "how to clean [lenses]" (care). → Each question is a prompt. Type each prompt word for word into ChatGPT and Google AI Mode more than once. Log the answer, whether you were mentioned or cited, and which sources it pulled. 2. Fix eligibility → OpenAI runs 3 crawlers. GPTBot is training, OAI-SearchBot is search inclusion, ChatGPT-User is user-triggered fetches. → OpenAI will commit a felony (Hugging Face hack) for training; they may ignore your bots.txt , but I don’t risk it. A broad WAF rule or a wildcard disallow should in theory stop these bots which you don’t want. → Robots.txt changes take roughly 24 hours to register on OpenAI's side. 3. Build a product truth layer → Put price, availability, variants, shipping and returns in visible HTML. Keep your Merchant Center feed matching the page. → Same problem as a Meta catalog throwing disapprovals when the feed and the PDP disagree on price. Same fix, wider blast radius. 4. Publish data only you have → Publish return reasons, support questions, product tests and sizing failures. → This is the single most underused asset in DTC. Use it for AEO, but also for creative. 5. Answer the follow-up questions → AI Mode queries average 3x the length of a traditional search. → One decision page should cover the answer, trade-offs, edge cases and next step. 6. Write an honest comparison page → Own "X vs Y" with a dated methodology, named criteria, and who shouldn't buy your product. 7. Keep product names consistent → Use the same brand, model and variant names everywhere. Otherwise the engine reads your old reviews, new listing and current SKU as 3 unrelated things. 8. Earn corroboration → Fix wrong facts on the review sites and forum threads already showing up in your answers from move 1. 9. Land citations on the right page → Deep-link citations to the relevant PDP or guide. A great ad pointed at a generic homepage underperforms a mediocre ad pointed at the right page. 10. Measure → Track AI visibility in Search Console, AI referrals in analytics, and citation rates on your question set, dated before and after. → Add an AI option to your post-purchase survey. When someone asks an assistant and walks straight to your site, there's no click to capture. Shout out to Lorea Lastiri for this playbook. I'm not an AEO expert, but she is!

posts.text: I've sold $450M of DTC products I see a NEW arbitrage for premium eCom: AppLovin Ads: → Placements inside mobile games and apps. → The ad takes the full screen. → Rewarded video: the user is locked in for 15-30 seconds to earn extra lives or in-game currency. → Interstitial: a 3-second unskippable window before the Skip button appears. A few years ago I would have laughed at putting a $60 physical product in the middle of someone's mobile game. Going into 2026 and 2027, these networks are performing well for premium eCom brands. (Especially those selling to 40 to 50 year old women.) But you need different creative for AppLovin: Rewarded video (locked in 15-30 seconds) → 0 to 25s: tell a story, show a satisfying demo, entertain them while they wait → 26 to 28s: build tension, this is the riser → 29 to 30s: strongest CTA, timed for the second before they can close it Interstitial (3-second window, then Skip appears) → Don't open on your hook. At second 0 they're annoyed and hunting for the X. → Reverse-engineer it. Seconds 0 to 3 build toward the hook. → The hook lands at second 3, the moment Skip becomes tappable. → This is the opposite of Meta where you're interrupting the scroll and trying to hook for the first 3 seconds. Cheatsheet: - Take your 3 best-performing Meta concepts - Recut the timing around the placement UI - Run rewarded and interstitial as separate tests - Judge the channel on blended MER, in-app attribution is messier than Meta's Anyone else testing AppLovin? posts.text: Most brands running Meta traffic to Amazon are optimizing for the wrong person. You can't fire a purchase event from Amazon back to Meta. So the campaign optimizes on the last thing it can see: the outbound click. Meta gets very good at finding people who click Amazon links. It has no idea which of them ever bought. I've managed $150M+ in Meta spend and this is the worst signal environment I deal with. Was talking through this with the founders at Jurni , who was willing to share some data on their learnings. Jurni's fix is a "Pre-retail landing experience" sitting between the ad and the PDP. What the page has to do: 1. Continue the ad, don't restart it. Same hook, same visual, same claim. If the page reintroduces the brand, you've reset the sale. 2. Handle the objection the PDP can't. On Amazon you're one tile in a grid of 40 competitors. The page is the only place you control the comparison. 3. One exit. No nav, no footer, no second offer. One button, deep linked to the right variant and pack size. Across their beauty and CPG customer set: - CPA down ~19% - ROAS up ~26% - 22% of ad traffic never clicks through to Amazon That third number is the one people react badly to. A fifth of your traffic dies on the page. That's the point though. That's low intent traffic getting filtered before it costs you an Amazon session. And now you have two segments you never had: people who clicked through, and people who didn't. Fire the first as your optimization event. Then it compounds. Higher-intent traffic on the PDP lifts conversion rate, and Amazon's ranking rewards conversion rate. You buy better traffic, and the algorithm hands you cheaper organic placement for it. Worth noting- these pages Jurni builds are AI-generated per-audience/per-ad variant, not one static page. That's part of why the objection-handling can be this specific: each version is built to match the exact ad it's continuing, and they're tracking performance per variant, not just in aggregate Caveat: this is their data across their customers, not mine, and CPA is in-platform. I'd want to see it hold in a geo test before I called it incremental.

posts.text: Can you scale on Meta ads? Plot your aMER versus your blended MER. Blended MER (bMER) = total revenue divided by total marketing spend. Acquisition MER (aMER) = new-customer revenue divided by acquisition spend. Two lines to plot against: → Sitting on the bMER = aMER diagonal means no repeat revenue to average in → Falling below aMER = 1 means you're buying customers at a loss Plot yourself and you land in one of four spots. Low bMER, low aMER → E.g. 1.6 bMER vs 0.9 aMER, nCAC $238, below the loss line → This is the brand scaling past breakeven. Every new customer costs you more than they're worth right now, and payback stretches past a year → Cut the worst 20-30% of spend, reset to the efficient core, rebuild through creative testing Low bMER, mid aMER → E.g. 2.3 bMER vs 2.1 aMER, 10% repeat customers, right on the bMER = aMER line → This is the leaky bucket. There's no repeat business to average in, so bMER barely clears aMER → Fix retention before you scale spend High bMER, low aMER → E.g. 6.0 bMER vs 1.3 aMER, 78% repeat customers → Left alone, Meta harvests the cheapest conversions available, and those conversions are people who were buying anyway → Rebuild prospecting with hooks written for cold traffic, accept a lower bMER for a quarter High bMER, high aMER → E.g. 8.4 bMER vs 4.6 aMER, marketing at 12% of revenue → This is the brand that's growing too efficiently. You need to spend more! → Keep spending until marginal aMER hits your LTV:CAC goal to grow quicker. What did I miss?

posts.text: I've run 20,000 ads and spent $150M on Meta . Benchmarks I've found over 6 years: 1. 1 new creative concept per $10k in monthly spend. At $500k/month that's 50 concepts (~3 ads per concept, more for static-heavy). 2. At $100k/mo, aim for 70% new concepts and 30% variations. As you scale past $1m/mo, max out at 50/50. But never drop below 50% new. 3. 70% of your creatives should be cut before week 2. Only 10-20% will ever hit your performance threshold. If you're keeping most of your ads alive, you're probably losing money. 4. Your top 1-2% of ads should drive 50% of total spend. If they don't, you haven't found real winners yet or you haven't utilized them well enough. 5. Big swings have lower hit rates (5-10%) but higher total potential. These are the ads that can scale to $1m+ in spend. 6. 70% video, 30% static for most ecom brands. New brands need more video (more education, less BOF audience). Clothing should lean heavier static (lots of SKUs to show). 7. 15-20% of budget goes to testing. Under 10% and your creative pipeline dries up. Over 25% and you're burning cash without enough scale behind winners. 8. When you 2x spend, expect 20-30% ROAS decline. A $30 CPA at $50k/month might become $40 at $200k. Scale requires better ads, better optimization, better structure, or lower targets. 9. Limit bid and budget changes to 25% max. For 90% of changes, smaller and more frequent changes outperform bigger ones. 10. Meta always targets returning customers. Aim to keep returning conversions under 15-20%. Accept it and plan around it. 11. Ad copy can improve performance up to 50%. But a great ad outperforms by 500%. Copy matters, but the creative itself is where the real leverage is. 12. A great media buyer improves ROAS 100%+ vs a bad one. Creative strategists make better decisions when they're working off clean data and with better media buyers, because the scaled ads are actual winners. Hope this helps. What others have I missed?

posts.text: HexClad Cookware runs ads at low revenue from Jan to Oct Makes 50% of their revenue in Nov/Dec How they stay disciplined and why: Who's HexClad? - Premium hybrid cookware (stainless steel + nonstick), sold DTC and in Costco - Gordon Ramsay and Fox invested $100M in 2024, valuing it over $1B - ~$170M revenue in 2022, on track for $350M in 2023, undisclosed after that (541% growth 2021-2024, #775 on Inc. 5000) How they run marketing for the 2-month sale: 1. Two-month sale → ~50% of revenue lands in November and December → 12% of it comes on Black Friday alone → $400 average order value, $699 for the 12-piece set 2. Consideration window → Under 20% of purchases happen inside a 7-day window → 80-85% of buyers say they knew HexClad for months first → Only ~26% of the country is ever "in market" for premium cookware 3. October loss → They run October MER 33% below their year-end target → The 13 days before the sale run about 50% below that → "That's going to allow us to spend into a full funnel" (Connor Rolain, Head of Growth) 4. Black Friday incrementality → ROAS lift peaks over 300% on Nov 12-13, before the sale opens → Black Friday weekend has the lowest lift of the whole period → Jason Panzer, President, left ~$1M of BFCM budget unspent: "It's bottom of funnel now. We did the work all throughout the year." 5. Forecast locked early → Offers, timing and targets set 15 weeks out → 85% of November revenue comes from the sale window → Set expectations to stay the course in October and build demand It's not easy to run marketing like HexClad. You need to have faith in your brand, and forecast incredibly well.

posts.text: Over the last 30 days, I've intentionally plummeted my LinkedIn impressions. It's made my consulting business 10x easier to run and way simpler. Here's why: For context, I run a one person consulting business for agency CEOs who want to build authority and inbound from decision makers. We use LinkedIn as an attention platform because that's where a lot of my client's decision makers or their sphere of influence lives. For my own business, I have no real reason to get loads of impressions and neither do my client's businesses. More just means more shit to sift through. More connection requests, more profile views, more DMs etc. So, here's how I've intentionally plummeted my LinkedIn impressions so I can spend more time with the right people and less time actually on LinkedIn: 1. I write a post that's for a specific person I know my ICP very well. I've worked with nearly 100 agency founders and CEOs by now, over the last 5 years. I can switch it on or off when I want to talk to them. Recently I've turned that switch well and truly on. And my engagement and impressions have plummeted. If that didn't happen, then my strategy wouldn't be working. When you write a post for specific person, you create more impact with that specific person you're trying to reach. And you put off the people you don't want to spend time with. 2. I get profile views & connection requests Naturally from these posts, people click to see my profile. And if they think I'm giving them value, they could hit connect with me too. These are incredible signals of intent / interest in me and my business that I can make sales from. But if I've got a post that goes viral and I get 500 connection requests from it, I have to go through those and find the good ones. That can take hours / days. Same goes for profile views. So it makes zero sense to go viral for what I'm trying to do - speak to agency founders and CEOs who are doing $500k to $10M/year. 3. I talk to them If I have a shorter, more targeted list of people who have viewed my profile and connected with me, then it gives me less people to talk to. Less people to talk to = less time spent talking to people = more time getting results for my clients. And it also = more time with my 6 month old daughter and wife who are everything to me. When I talk to people, I make more money. So if I can talk to less people and talk to the right people, I'm using my time very efficiently. My client's need the same approach. Agency founders and CEOs are busy, running small teams and caring for their high profile clients. They don't need to waste time talking to freebie seekers. TL;DR: The opportunity you have on LinkedIn to find your exact ICP, is truly insane. Don't make it harder for yourself by attracting MORE people. Do everything you can to attract the RIGHT ones.

posts.text: I spend $6M/mo on Google ads There are 4 types of incrementality studies you can run with them Brand Lift: → Survey-based test that measures whether the ad moved recall, awareness, consideration, favorability, or purchase intent → Runs on YouTube Video and Demand Gen campaigns → Needs $10,000 in spend over a 10-day window Search Lift: → Measures whether people searched for your brand after seeing the ad → Runs on the same Video and Demand Gen campaigns as Brand Lift → Rides alongside a Brand Lift study at no extra budget Conversion Lift based on users: → Splits your audience into people who saw the ad and a holdout who didn't → Native on Video and Demand Gen, needs a Google rep to set up on Search, Shopping, Display, or PMax → Gives directional results from $5,000 in spend and 1,000 conversions → Relies mostly on opt-in traffic, which brings its own measurement gaps Conversion Lift based on geography: → Splits regions on and off instead of individual users → Counts both online and offline conversions → Spans Search, Shopping, PMax, Video, Display, Demand Gen, and App → Needs a Google rep, and the geo split is noisier with no demographic breakdown Got $10,000 and 10 days? Run Brand Lift and Search Lift together. Got $5,000 and 1,000 conversions? Run Conversion Lift based on users. Need offline conversions counted? Run Conversion Lift based on geography. Note- a Google lift study is Google measuring Google. Pair the result with a holdout test of your own for greater impartiality. Hope this helps.

posts.text: Google ads over holidays periods can suck. How to forecast performance & adjust bids in advance. 1. Holidays carry CVR risk → Traffic changes over holiday periods. B2B search volume thins out over Thanksgiving week and between Christmas and New Year because buyers are off work. Retail volume spikes into Black Friday and Cyber Monday, then drops off. → Volume on its own doesn't hurt CPA, since you pay per click and Google bids per auction. People keep clicking but delay the purchase, so the drop lands in conversion rate first. → Smart Bidding sets each bid from auction signals and accounts for conversion delay. A sharp CVR drop over a few days can land before bids catch up, and you pay pre-holiday prices for holiday clicks. → E.g. a hypothetical account at a $10 CPC and 5% CVR runs a $200 CPA. If CVR slips to 4% over a 4-day holiday weekend and CPC holds, CPA comes in at $250 for those 4 days. → Holding a $200 CPA on a 4% CVR takes an $8 CPC. A -20% conversion rate adjustment pushes bids toward that $8 but doesn't guarantee a 20% lower CPC. Set the change ahead of the window, through the seasonality adjustment in step 2 or a manual bid cut on campaigns that don't use Smart Bidding. 2. Seasonality adjustments for short windows → A seasonality adjustment tells Smart Bidding ahead of time that conversion rates will move over a set date range. → Don't set a seasonality adjustment for every holiday. Smart Bidding already accounts for normal seasonality. Use the adjustment for a significant, short-lived CVR change you have a reason to expect. → Find it under the Tools icon, then Budgets and bidding, then Adjustments, then the Seasonal tab. Hit the plus button and pick Conversion rate. → Set the start and end dates, choose which campaigns it covers, and enter the conversion rate change you expect. For the hypothetical 5% to 4% drop above, enter -20%. → Keep the adjustment to events of 1 to 7 days. Google says seasonality adjustments may be less effective over longer periods. → The adjustment reverts automatically once the end date passes. 3. Read lag before reacting → Conversion lag is the gap between the click you pay for and the conversion Google reports against it. A form fill lands the same day. A signed deal can take weeks. → Holidays stretch that gap. People click on the Wednesday and buy after the long weekend. B2B buyers click before the break and convert once the office reopens. → E.g. the 4% CVR in the hypothetical above can be understated. Conversions from holiday clicks get reported after the weekend and the 4% climbs. → Pull your time-to-conversion report before the window (Goals, then Measurement, then Attribution) so you know how long your lag runs. → Wait out that lag before judging the holiday week. Hope this helps.
posts.headline: Google ads over holidays periods can suck.

posts.text: 6 weeks ago, Google changed how bidding works I checked 120 accounts to see what happened: CONTEXT - Before August 17, a budget-limited campaign with a $100 target CPA always tried to find the cheapest conversions. So if it ran out of budget it might have a CPA of $70. - Since August 17, Google bids up to the target CPA. So even if you run out of budget, you'll hit $100 CPA. - Target ROAS works the same way. A campaign beating its ROAS target gets pulled back down to the target. - Note: some of these 120 ad accounts we manage, some we don't. I split every campaign into three groups and compared 28 days before against 28 days after: 1. Budget-limited and beating target CPA 2. Budget-limited but already at target CPA 3. No target or no budget limit The campaigns that were budget-limited and beating target CPA - CPA up 63% - CPC up 20% - Conversions down 22% Campaigns that were budget-limited but already at target CPA: - CPA down 6% - CPC up 1% - Conversions down 1% The control group barely moved either: - CPC up 3% - CPA up 3% - Conversions down 1% What this means: If you're not actively managing your account, and ensuring you minimize Search Lost IS (Budget) by adjusting budgets and target CPA / ROAS, you will overpay for your conversions. (None of our client fit into this bucket) Hope this helps
posts.headline: 6 weeks ago, Google changed how bidding works

posts.text: Where does PMax actually spend? Pulled 365 days of data from 53 accounts: 1. Search → Median account: 61% of PMax spend goes to Search → The range across all 53: 2% to 99% → Above 90%, PMax is a glorified Search campaign (I audited one at 82% and Search had under 30 conversions a month) → On our accounts we pull converting search terms out of PMax into Search until the search portion drops below 10% 2. Search Partners → Median: 3% of spend → We launched one PMax campaign where it took 30% (it got calls, but no qualified leads) → No campaign-level toggle exists to turn it off. Keep an eye on this 3. YouTube and Display → Medians: 10% and 3% → Individual accounts push over 80% into YouTube → Google allocates from your assets, audience signals and conversion data → Repurpose your Meta ads into the asset groups to start (statics too, no re-edits). That's how we launch every client and performance holds → If YouTube CPA comes in near Search, that's your case to invest in proper YouTube creative 4. Gmail, Discover and Maps → Median: 0% across nearly all 53 accounts → One account has 84% of its PMax spend going to Maps 5. Why no benchmark exists → Google gives you no channel-level budget control (their own docs say to influence the mix through assets, signals and exclusions) → Channel reporting only rolled out to every PMax campaign in November 2025, and to MCC level in December Summary - 61% median Search share, with a 2% to 99% range - High Search share means PMax is duplicating your Search campaign - Search Partners needs a manual account-level exclusion - Pull the channel report on your own account before assuming it's typical Hope this helps

posts.text: How to steal competitor revenue With Google Demand Gen ads: 1. Catch the switchers → Target the queries people use when they're trying to leave: "alternatives to [competitor]", "[competitor] pricing", "[competitor] complaints", "cheaper than [competitor]". → These people aren't shopping. They're already looking for a way out. → You reach them on cheap inventory instead of paying premium CPCs on the competitor's brand term. 2. Competitor-search audiences → Build a custom segment with the "people who searched for any of these terms on Google" option. Drop in every competitor name plus the switch terms from step 1. → Serve across YouTube, Discover and Gmail. The click costs a fraction of a brand-term search click. → Once it's converting, build a lookalike off the converters to scale past the original audience. 3. Sell the weakness → You can't put a competitor's trademark in the ad copy, so don't try. → Lead with the thing they're frustrated by: price, support, slow onboarding, contract lock-in. Let the audience targeting do the matching. 4. One ad group per pain → Don't dump every angle into one group. Split it: a pricing group, a support group, a lock-in group. → Each group points at a page that proves you fix that one thing. 5. Landing page match → Build a page on the exact differentiator, with social proof and the numbers to back it. Cheatsheet: → Bid on the exit queries → Build a "searched for these terms on Google" custom segment, then run YouTube, Discover and Gmail → Layer a lookalike off the converters to scale → Sell the frustration: price, support, onboarding, lock-in. → One ad group per pain → Match the landing page to the exact differentiator

posts.text: We ran a direct mail campaign that generated 4,600 leads and 450 opportunities for a $1,500 offer. How you can too Results: → Roughly 375,000 mail pieces sent over the program → About 4,600 leads → About 450 campaign-attributed opportunities, roughly 1 in 10 leads → Roughly $1M in influenced pipeline 1. Audiences → We split the list into four audiences, the house file, previous responders, competitor audiences, and intent-based prospect lists. → Each audience got its own drop and its own campaign in Salesforce so we could compare cost per opportunity head to head. → House file and previous responders came in cheaper per opportunity than the broad prospect lists. → A previous responder had already replied to the brand once, so the piece read as a follow-up. 2. Tracking → Every piece carried a mailer-specific URL, a QR code, and UTM tags. → Salesforce logged the campaign attribution on every lead that came through a mailer link. → We matched back CRM records for responders who came in through another channel after the piece landed. → A QR scan alone does not tell you whether a piece acquired a customer profitably, so every audience was judged on cost per opportunity after the same maturation window. 3. Mailer creative and offer → We send a handwritten style letter for a B2B offer as we tend to see higher conversion rates versus a postcard. → We adjust copy by segment. For example, a previous responder gets a reminder of what they looked at before, and a competitor list audience member gets a switching offer. → Every piece carries one offer and one call to action. The reader scans the QR code or types the short URL. Summary: → Split the list by audience type and track each one on its own campaign. → Put a URL, QR code, and UTM on every piece and matchback the rest. → Judge audiences on cost per opportunity after the same window. → Put one offer and one call to action on a letter written to the segment. Hope this helps

posts.text: Is one Google ad group taking ALL the spend? And NOT testing your other keywords? How to kickstart starved ad groups: 1. Rank and budget Search Lost IS (Rank): → If it's high, bids and quality score are the constraint. Fix those first. → If it's low, the starved ad group wins the auctions it enters. Search Lost IS (Budget): → If it's high, the campaign is capped. Raise the cap and the extra budget still flows to the dominant ad group. → If it's low, the campaign was never capped, and the starvation sits in how budget splits between ad groups. Either way, every ad group inherits the campaign's target CPA, and shared budget typically concentrates on the ad group with the deepest conversion history. 2. Fix the bid strategy first → Confirm the campaign runs Target CPA. Maximize Conversions gives no ad-group-level lever. → Raise the target CPA on the starved ad group. The override gives Smart Bidding permission to enter more auctions there, above the shared campaign default. → Raise the campaign budget cap next, so the ad group you unlocked doesn't get re-capped the moment it spends. 3. Overshoot the target CPA on purpose → On a low-spend ad group, set the target CPA above what you want, buying more auctions and more signal on what converts. → Pull the search term report while the overshoot runs and add negatives aggressively, or the spend lands on queries you don't want. Summary: → Check rank loss and budget loss together first → Switch the campaign to Target CPA → Raise the target on the starved ad group → Raise the campaign budget cap straight after → Add negatives while the overshoot runs A shared budget typically concentrates on the deepest conversion history by default. A target CPA override is how you move that budget somewhere else.

Listen to this.... Last week I was on Q&A call and someone asked what I thought about writing posts with a broad hook and a hard sell at the end. Personally? I would not do this. If you sell high-ticket, there is no reason to go broad. No reason at all. You need one or two of the right people. Not 100 of well, anyone. If you get the wrong inbound, it just means getting on tons of sales calls where the person is never in a position to afford what you sell. Imagine: You get 50,000 impressions from a post. posts.text: I tested Jev on negative Google ad keywords. Results are actually quite surprising. Jev is a new AI decision model that launched in early access on Sept 15. We tested it against a very mature AI workflow we have that identifies irrelevant keywords being bid for on Google ads and then removes them from campaigns. TEST: → Jev vs our tool (culmination of 2 years of iteration) → Jev and our tool each decided which search terms to block. → We scored both against a Claude review of every term. → Neither tool had context on the account outside of the website URL, to make it a fair read. Where Jev won → Jev caught 165 of the 292 junk terms. Our tool caught 39. → Jev cost $0.14 per 1,000 search terms. Our tool costs $2.68. Where Jev lost → Jev blocked 119 good search terms. Our tool blocked 35. → For every $1 of junk spend Jev removed, Jev blocked $2.60 of good spend. → Blocking a good term cuts off a source of leads which is worse than saving money. → Our tool marked 691 of 731 verdicts high confidence. Most of Jev's confidence scores sat between 0.2 and 0.6, close to a coin flip. Jev is cheap enough to try as a first-pass filter. But we're still keeping our search term tool. Has anyone else tested Jev on search terms yet?
